title: Deadlock Prevention
summary: Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions at once — prevention means structurally guaranteeing that at least one of them can never hold, and lock ordering is the version you'll actually use.

slides.markdown:
If deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions ([mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait](deadlock-fundamentals)) simultaneously, then breaking **any single one** structurally, so it can never hold, makes deadlock provably impossible in that system — not just unlikely.

That's **prevention**: a design-time guarantee, not a runtime check. This topic walks through attacking each of the four conditions, why three of them are usually impractical to attack directly, and why global lock ordering (attacking circular wait) is the one every working engineer actually reaches for.

slides.sectionTitle: The prevention strategy: guarantee one condition can never hold
slides.markdown:
Prevention is a structural guarantee baked into the system's design — a rule enforced at all times, not something checked at request time (that's avoidance, the next topic) or fixed up after the fact (that's detection and recovery). Because deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions simultaneously, eliminating even one makes the whole thing structurally impossible: there's no combination of timing or bad luck that can produce a deadlock if one of its four necessary ingredients is permanently unavailable.

The trade-off across all four options below is the same shape every time: the condition you attack determines what flexibility or performance you give up in exchange for the guarantee.

slides.sectionTitle: Attacking mutual exclusion — not always possible
slides.markdown:
Eliminating mutual exclusion means making the resource shareable instead of exclusive — if nobody ever needs sole access, there's nothing to deadlock over. This genuinely works for read-only resources: a file opened read-only by multiple processes, or a read replica multiple clients query concurrently, needs no exclusive lock at all.

But it fails outright for anything that's inherently exclusive by nature: a printer can't physically print two documents interleaved, a bank account's balance can't be safely updated by two writers at once without exclusion, a write lock on a database row exists precisely because concurrent unsynchronized writes corrupt data. For these, mutual exclusion isn't a design choice you can remove — it's a correctness requirement, which is why this is the least generally applicable of the four attack points.

slides.sectionTitle: Attacking hold-and-wait — acquire upfront or release before requesting
slides.markdown:
Two variants. **Acquire all resources upfront**: a process must request and be granted every resource it will ever need before starting any work, all at once — if it can't get all of them, it gets none and waits, so it's never simultaneously holding one resource while blocked waiting for another. **Release before requesting**: a process must give up everything it currently holds before requesting something new.

Both genuinely eliminate hold-and-wait, but at a real cost: upfront acquisition requires knowing your full resource needs in advance (often impossible for interactive or data-dependent workloads) and can badly hurt utilization — a process holding a resource it won't touch for another ten minutes, just because it needed to grab everything at once, blocks other processes from using it in the meantime. Release-before-requesting can cause the same critical section's logic to need re-validation after re-acquiring, since state may have changed while the resource was released.

slides.sectionTitle: Attacking no-preemption — forcibly taking resources back
slides.markdown:
If a process holding some resources requests another that isn't available, one option is to forcibly **preempt** — take away — the resources it already holds, rather than let it sit blocked while holding them. The process's held resources go back into the pool, and it has to re-acquire everything (including what it lost) later, typically after being rolled back to some safe point.

This works well for resources whose state can be cleanly saved and restored — CPU registers (this is quite literally what a context switch already does — see Context Switching) or memory pages (which can be swapped out and back in). It works badly for resources where mid-operation preemption is destructive or meaningless — you can't "preempt" a printer halfway through printing a physical page, or a database transaction that's partway through an irreversible external side effect (like having already sent a confirmation email).

slides.sectionTitle: Attacking circular wait — global lock ordering
slides.markdown:
Assign every lockable resource in the system a fixed, total order (often just alphabetical by name, or by memory address, or an explicit numeric rank assigned when each lock is created) and enforce a single rule everywhere: **always acquire locks in increasing order**, never the reverse, regardless of which code path you're in.

With that rule, circular wait becomes structurally impossible: a cycle would require some process to be waiting for a lower-ranked lock while holding a higher-ranked one, which the rule forbids outright — you simply can never construct the chain. This is the prevention strategy that's actually practical and widely used in real code, precisely because it doesn't require knowing resource needs in advance (unlike attacking hold-and-wait) and doesn't require resources to be preemptible (unlike attacking no-preemption) — it's a pure discipline about acquisition order.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: fixing the two-lock deadlock with consistent ordering
Diagram: lock ordering as a DAG that prevents cycles
slides.markdown:
![Global lock ordering as a DAG](assets/lock-ordering-dag.svg)

This is the same idea as the resource allocation graph from Deadlock Fundamentals, but constrained by design: as long as every acquisition follows the fixed rank order, the resulting "who might wait for whom" graph is guaranteed to stay a DAG (directed acyclic graph) — and a DAG, by definition, cannot contain a cycle. Circular wait isn't just unlikely under this rule, it's mathematically ruled out.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: cost/practicality of attacking each of the four conditions
slides.markdown:
| Condition attacked | Practicality | Typical cost |
|---|---|---|
| Mutual exclusion | Low — only works for genuinely shareable resources | N/A where exclusion is required for correctness |
| Hold and wait | Moderate — works but needs upfront resource knowledge | Reduced concurrency/utilization, possible starvation of large requests |
| No preemption | Moderate — works only for cleanly-preemptible resources | Rollback/re-acquisition overhead, unusable for irreversible operations |
| Circular wait (lock ordering) | High — broadly applicable, low runtime cost | Requires discipline across the whole codebase; one violation anywhere breaks the guarantee |

**How to decide:** default to global lock ordering wherever you control all the code paths — it's the cheapest and most broadly applicable. Fall back to hold-and-wait or no-preemption attacks only for the specific cases (transactional systems with rollback support, resources with known-in-advance usage) where they fit naturally.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: partial lock ordering — one code path forgets the convention
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We follow lock ordering in all our main code paths, so we're safe from deadlock."

**Why it's wrong:** lock ordering is an **all-or-nothing** guarantee — it only prevents circular wait if *every* code path that acquires more than one of the ordered locks follows the rule, with zero exceptions. A single utility function, a rarely-hit error-handling branch, or a third-party library callback that acquires the same two locks in reverse order reintroduces circular wait exactly as if there were no rule at all — and because it's rare, it often survives testing and only shows up under production load.

**Correct model:** treat lock ordering as a codebase-wide invariant that needs enforcement, not just a convention documented in a comment. Real teams enforce this with tooling — Linux kernel's `lockdep` tracks actual lock acquisition order at runtime and flags any inconsistency immediately, even if it never actually deadlocks in that run; some languages provide similar lint rules or runtime checkers. Treat any detected ordering violation as a bug to fix immediately, not a theoretical risk to note and move on from.
